summary: Specifies how OSPFv2 routing extensions meet the routing requirements of the ITU-T Automatically Switched Optical Network architecture, working with the GMPLS control plane for optical transport networks.

eli5.summary: Phone company cables made of light need a map to find paths. This teaches an existing map-sharing protocol to meet the special rules of those light networks.

subtitle: OSPFv2 extensions that let optical transport networks advertise their reachability and links, level by level.

tldr.problem: The ITU-T ASON architecture needs a routing protocol that can describe transport nodes, hierarchical routing areas and multi-layer links, which plain OSPF traffic engineering does not cover.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds sub-TLVs to OSPFv2 TE LSAs to name transport nodes by TE Router ID and to tag information exported up or down the routing hierarchy, and it reuses the Node Attribute TLV for reachability.
tldr.outcome: It moves RFC 5787 from Experimental to the Standards Track, obsoletes it, and updates RFC 5786. It is scoped to the ITU-T Recommendations current when RFC 4258 and RFC 4652 were written.

today: RFC 6827 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 5787 and updates RFC 5786.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The ITU-T defines the architecture of the Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON). The GMPLS protocol suite (RFC 3945) is designed to provide a control plane for networks such as SONET/SDH, Optical Transport Networks and lambda switching networks. RFC 4258 sets out the routing requirements for GMPLS to support ASON, and RFC 4652 evaluates the IETF link state protocols against them.

This document describes the OSPFv2 specifics. It processes the generic link attributes of RFC 3630, RFC 4202 and RFC 4203 and extends them. Technology-specific attributes may be defined elsewhere.

The work is scoped to the requirements and evaluation in RFC 4258 and RFC 4652 and to the ITU-T Recommendations that were current when they were written. The RFC says future revisions may be needed if those Recommendations change.
sections.eli5: Some phone networks send data as flashes of light and need their own kind of map. This document explains how to use an existing map-sharing method for them.

sections.title: Routing Areas and OSPF Areas
sections.content:
An ASON routing area (RA) is a partition of the transport plane. RAs are nested: a parent RA contains child RAs, which may themselves contain RAs. Links inside an RA are internal; links connecting RAs are external. The internal links of a child RA MAY be hidden from the parent.

An RA can be mapped to an OSPF area, but the hierarchy of RA levels does not map to the hierarchy of OSPF areas. Instead, successive levels MUST be represented by separate OSPF protocol instances, and information moves between levels by export and import between those instances. An RA is identified by the combination of its OSPF Instance ID and Area ID. With careful network-wide configuration, the Area ID alone can do the job, and the RFC RECOMMENDS this.
sections.eli5: Think of a country with states, and states with towns. Each level keeps its own map, and the levels pass notes up and down instead of sharing one giant map.

sections.title: Mapping ASON to OSPF Terms
sections.content:
An ASON transport node corresponds to one OSPF TE node. It is identified by the TE Router Address TLV from RFC 3630, which this document calls the TE Router ID. That is not the same as the OSPF Router ID, which identifies an OSPF router in the control plane. The Router Address TLV gives a stable IP address that is reachable whenever there is IP connectivity to the node.

ASON defines a Routing Controller (RC), which handles routing information, and a Protocol Controller (PC), which handles protocol message exchanges. An OSPF router advertising ASON TE topology performs both functions. Because the control-plane adjacency topology and the transport topology need not be congruent, one OSPF router MUST be able to advertise for several transport nodes.
sections.eli5: A telephone exchange and the clerk who reports on it can be different. Here one clerk, the OSPF router, can report for several machines, so each machine needs its own name tag.

sections.title: Reachability, Links and New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
For reachability, the Node Attribute TLV of RFC 5786 advertises a TE Router ID together with the address prefixes reachable from that transport node. Because one router may speak for several nodes, a Node Attribute TLV MAY appear in more than one TE LSA from the same RC. This relaxes the RFC 5786 rule.

For links, the attribute mapping to Link TLV sub-TLVs is unchanged, except for local adaptation. Adaptation and termination capabilities are advertised in two separate Interface Switching Capability Descriptor (ISCD) sub-TLVs (type 15) of the same Link TLV. For example, a link between an optical cross-connect and an IP/MPLS router carries one ISCD for lambda switching termination and one for packet switching adaptation. Advertisements SHOULD be done per layer.

Two new sub-TLVs name transport nodes. The Local and Remote TE Router ID sub-TLV (type 10, length 8) goes in the Link TLV, and the Local TE Router ID sub-TLV (type 5, length 4) goes in the Node Attribute TLV. Both MUST be included when ASON information is advertised, and a value of 0 is not allowed. If the Link sub-TLV is missing or has a zero value, that link is not used for transport-plane path computation and the condition SHOULD be logged. When present, it identifies the link endpoints and the Link-ID sub-TLV MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: Each machine gets a name tag, and each wire says which two name tags it connects. If a tag is missing or blank, nobody trusts that wire.

sections.title: Exporting Information Between Levels
sections.content:
RCs supporting RAs at more than one level pass information up and down by importing and exporting TE LSAs, which are area-scoped Opaque LSAs with Opaque type 1. The Router Address, Link and Node Attribute top-level TLVs MAY be exchanged. The content MAY be filtered or aggregated, as long as the result stays consistent. In practice only reachability, and link topology under strict policy control, is expected to be exchanged. This mechanism is not OSPF ABR functionality and does not make OSPF areas hierarchical.

When several RCs export between the same levels, information could be re-advertised back into the RA it came from. To prevent that loop, the Inter-RA Export Upward (type 12) and Inter-RA Export Downward (type 13) sub-TLVs, each of length 4 and carrying an RA ID, tag exported information.

The rules are two. Anything tagged Downward, meaning it came from above, MUST NOT be exported upward. Anything tagged Upward MUST NOT be exported downward into the RA whose ID it carries, since a parent RA may contain several child RAs. The tags MUST be retained when the information is passed on.
sections.eli5: When town news goes up to the state and then back down, you do not want it returned to the town that sent it. A small label on each note says where it came from, so the note is never sent back.

sections.title: Scalability and Management
sections.content:
These extensions apply only to ASON routing domains and are not expected to be combined with global Internet or Layer 3 VPN routing. An RC that must join both would use separate OSPFv2 instances. Because a multi-level hierarchy could produce a lot of information, RCs MUST follow three limits. By default, the exchange between adjacent RAs is limited to reachability, and prefix aggregation is RECOMMENDED. Exchange involving TE attributes MUST be under strict policy control, with pacing and thresholds for triggered updates strongly RECOMMENDED. The number of routing levels MUST also be under strict policy control.

If the RA ID is mapped to the OSPF Area ID, OSPF itself isolates RAs, since packets are accepted only when the area ID matches the interface. For topology changes, OSPF flooding and purging of Opaque LSAs handles adding and removing reachability information, and stale LSAs SHOULD NOT be used unless the advertising RC is reachable. Section 12 of the RFC also tabulates how the document meets each requirement of RFC 4258.
sections.eli5: To stop the mail room being flooded, neighbors only swap the most useful information by default, and the bosses decide when to share more.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The TE LSA extensions in this document are not used for SPF computation and have no direct effect on IP routing. ASON routing domains are bounded by the usual administrative boundaries, and the mechanisms that secure normal OSPF LSAs can be applied equally to TE LSAs. The RFC points to OSPF cryptographic authentication and to RFC 5709, which uses HMAC with the SHA family.

RCs that export or import ASON information between RAs MUST also apply policy control to the maximum amount of information advertised and the maximum rate. The goal is to limit the damage a compromised RC can do to the RAs it is attached to.
sections.eli5: Use the same locks you use for normal OSPF messages. Also limit how much each helper can pass along, so one bad helper cannot flood everyone.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned new sub-TLV types in three registries. The Link TLV gets Local and Remote TE Router ID (10), Inter-RA Export Upward (12) and Inter-RA Export Downward (13). The Node Attribute TLV gets Local TE Router ID (5), plus 12 and 13. The Router Address TLV had no sub-TLVs, so a new registry was created for it, and 12 and 13 are assigned there. Types 0 to 32767 in that registry are assigned by Standards Action, with type 0 reserved. The values for 12 and 13 MUST be the same in all three TLVs.
sections.eli5: The official number list now includes these new labels, with the same number for the same label everywhere.
